user_message: What usually happens after a red day?

author.intent: No ticker named, so the default (SPY), said. On the session after a day that closed down, what the price typically did (the usual move and path of that next session).
author.if_asked: SPY. Red day means it closed lower than the day before.
author.also_fine: Red day read as closing below its own open, if that is said.

stage_1_what_strata_did.reading_shown: On SPY, after the previous session closed down: how the price moved from the open to the close.
assumed_shown: No ticker was named, so SPY is used.

answers.headline: After the previous session closed down, SPY moved +0.01% on average from the open to the close (median +0.06%), over 3,894 days.
what_happened: It ended higher than it started on 52.5% of those days.
Half of the days ended between -0.48% and +0.53%; the furthest it typically ran in its favour was +0.47% and against it -0.52% (medians).
The average could be off: the range it is likely in runs from -0.02% to +0.05%, which includes zero.

user_message: When does SPY normally make its high?

author.intent: SPY: at what time of day the session's high is usually made (the distribution of the time of the day's high).
author.if_asked: The time of day of the day's high, over all the history you have.

stage_1_what_strata_did.reading_shown: On SPY: when the session's high was made, in 30-minute parts of the session.

answers.headline: SPY made its high of the day between 09:30 and 10:00 on 24.4% of sessions, more than any other half hour; the next most common was 15:30–16:00 (23.3%).
what_happened: If the high could fall anywhere, each part of the day would hold about 7.7%.
Counted on 2,741 sessions from Jan 2016 to Nov 2026 (New York time).
answers.why_it_matters: The open and the close are where the day's extremes cluster: a level set in the middle of the day is usually not the day's high or low.

independent_check.text: Recalculated independently from the one-minute bars: the same 2,741 sessions and the same figure in every part of the day.

what_this_cannot_tell_you: Only whole sessions of one-minute bars are used; a session the provider holds in part is left out.

user_message: Does the first hour tell you anything about the rest of the day?

author.intent: No ticker named, so the default (SPY), said. Whether the direction of the first hour of the session (9:30 to 10:30 New York) goes with the direction of the rest of the session after it.
author.if_asked: SPY. First hour up or down against the rest of the day up or down.

stage_1_what_strata_did.reading_shown: On SPY: how often the direction of the first 60-minute candle matches the rest of the session after it.

answers.headline: The first 60-minute candle matched the direction of the rest of the session 51.8% of the time, about what two unrelated directions would give.
what_happened: If the two directions were unrelated they would match about 50.3% of the time; the measured rate's likely range is 49.9% to 53.7%.
Simply guessing "up" every day would have matched the rest of the session 54.9% of the time, which is better than following the candle.

numbers.label: Matched the rest of the day

independent_check.text: Recalculated independently from the stored bars: every agreement count is the same.

what_this_cannot_tell_you: Only sessions with intraday bars can be measured: 2,730 of them, 2016-01-04 to 2026-11-27.
Direction only: a session that closes one cent above its open counts the same as one that closes 2% above it. Nothing here says how far the session went.

stage_1_what_strata_did.reading_shown: On SPY: the average move from open to close, by weekday.

answers.headline: Fridays on SPY averaged -0.015% from the open to the close, against +0.012% on the other days: slightly worse, but well within what chance produces, so Fridays are not reliably bad. (1,705 Fridays.)
